entries.rationale: Measured across the first three batches (M1-M3), every real member defect was caught by a hygiene or typecheck gate and none was first caught by the integration suites. Running the cheap gates to completion before the expensive run turned 75-minute discoveries into seconds.

entries.anchor: Step 3: Run the expensive verification ONCE, and read its result in four states
entries.rationale: A two-way verdict (repair or evict) would twice have reverted correct member work: the failures came from a shared cross-machine Atlas test pool, not the code. automation-broken must block and capability-unavailable must skip; neither may evict.

entries.anchor: Step 4b: Which model decides — a different axis from tier
entries.rationale: Escalation is split by authority, not difficulty: the parent repairs mechanical failures, a member-tier model decides semantic ones. In M3 a USD 1.77, 8-minute member-tier escalation outperformed the parent's own judgement, and the parent's 'trivial' pluralization fix took three attempts.

entries.anchor: If rebase-merge is refused, ship with a MERGE COMMIT — never a squash.
entries.rationale: M3 needed four base merges over five hours; GitHub then refused rebase-merge because the branch carried merge commits, and a local rebase re-conflicted since the resolutions lived in those merges. The real requirement is that per-issue commits survive for eviction, revert and bisect. A merge commit satisfies it; a squash never does.

Squash was ruled out twice over: it destroys the per-issue commits attribution depends on, and GitHub's default squash body re-imports every wip commit subject carrying a skip-ci marker, which silently suppressed the push event on main and the npm publish for PR #602.

The first scheduler-driven batch showed the batch path read the in-progress claim marker but never wrote or released it, so two prep runs would select the same issues. Prep now claims at manifest time; integrate must release on every disposal, supersession included, or claims leak forever.
